claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid and compositionally homogeneous.
Surface segregation of the lowest-melting constituent governs the onset and progression of the phase transition.
Enrichment of the lowest-melting constituent at the nanoparticle surface locally reduces the melting temperature.
Melting initiates at the enriched surface and subsequently propagates inward.
An inert passivating coating can inhibit surface segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Elevated temperature causes the lower-melting constituent to segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Native-surface nanoparticles will begin melting at the surface earlier than passivated nanoparticles under an identical temperature ramp.
Passivated nanoparticles will exhibit delayed or more spatially homogeneous melting relative to native-surface nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios under inert-atmosphere conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not directly apply to bulk materials or nanoparticles in reactive environments.
Atomic diffusion kinetics may contribute to the transition but are secondary to surface segregation under the stated conditions.
Indistinguishable melting onset and progression in coated and native nanoparticles would falsify the proposed surface-segregation mechanism.
